claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical observations in ALS patients.

claims.claim: Oculomotor and trochlear motor neurons are more resistant than SpMNs to neurodegeneration in the ALS mouse model expressing human (h) SOD1 G93A.
claims.source: Oculomotor and trochlear motor neurons are also more resistant than SpMNs to neurodegeneration in the ALS mouse model expressing human (h) SOD1 G93A (Haenggeli and Kato, 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haenggeli and Kato, 2002.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of ALS patients suffer from sporadic ALS while approximately 10% of ALS cases are familial.
claims.source: With shared clinical manifestations, ~90% of patients suffer from sporadic ALS while ~10% of ALS cases are familial.
claims.evidence: This is a well-established epidemiological fact about ALS.

claims.claim: More than fifty genes involved in different biological processes have been reported to contribute to familial ALS cases.
claims.source: More than fifty genes involved in different biological processes have been reported to contribute to the familial ALS cases. (Rosen, 1993; Taylor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rosen, 1993 and Taylor et al., 2016.

claims.claim: One common hallmark found in both familial and sporadic ALS is the accumulation of aggregated proteins.
claims.source: One common hallmark found in both familial and sporadic ALS is the accumulation of aggregated proteins, which is also shared by many other neurodegenerative diseases (Yerbury et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yerbury et al., 2016.

claims.claim: ALS mutations in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and C9ORF72 generate proteins with a propensity to misfold and aggregate.
claims.source: ALS mutations in SOD1, TARDBP (TAR DNA-binding protein 43 kDa), FUS (Fused in Sarcoma) and C9ORF72 generate proteins with a propensity to misfold and aggregate (Bruijn et al., 1998; Neumann et al., 2006; Deng et al., 2010; Zu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on ALS-causing mutations.

claims.claim: In both ALS patients and mouse models, SpMNs and astrocytes typically contain inclusions positive for ubiquitinated proteins and the ubiquitin-binding protein SQSTM1 (p62).
claims.source: In both ALS patients and mouse models, SpMNs and astrocytes typically contain inclusions positive for ubiquitinated proteins and the ubiquitin-binding protein SQSTM1 (Sequestosome 1, also known as p62) (Leigh et al., 1991; Watanabe et al., 2001; Mizuno et al., 2006; Neumann et al., 2006; Gal et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies documenting protein inclusions in ALS.

claims.claim: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system.
claims.source: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system, while large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway (Dikic, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dikic, 2017 and represents established knowledge about protein degradation pathways.

claims.claim: Large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway.
claims.source: Soluble and misfolded proteins are degraded primarily by the ubiquitin proteasome system, while large protein aggregates are recognized and removed by the autophagy lysosome pathway (Dikic, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dikic, 2017 and represents established knowledge about protein degradation pathways.

claims.claim: ALS-causing misfolding proteins, like mutant SOD1, can be degraded by both the proteasome and autophagy pathways.
claims.source: Therefore, ALS-causing misfolding proteins, like mutant SOD1, can be degraded by both the proteasome and autophagy pathways (Kabuta et al., 2006; Castillo et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kabuta et al., 2006 and Castillo et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Mutations in genes encoding important components of degradation pathways can cause ALS, including UBQLN2, SQSTM1 (p62), OPTN, VCP, VAPB and TBK1.
claims.source: Moreover, mutations in genes encoding important components of these degradation pathways can cause ALS (Taylor et al., 2016; Ghasemi and Brown, 2018), including UBQLN2 (Deng et al., 2011), SQSTM1 (p62) (Fecto et al., 2011; Rubino et al., 2012; Hirano et al., 2013), OPTN (Maruyama et al., 2010), VCP (Johnson et al., 2010), VAPB (Nishimura et al., 2004) and TBK1 (Freischmidt et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies identifying ALS-causing mutations in degradation pathway genes.

claims.claim: Matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP-9) is expressed only in the fast-fatigable α-motor neurons, a selective subtype of SpMNs vulnerable in ALS.
claims.source: Matrix metallopeptidase 9 (MMP-9) is expressed only in the fast-fatigable α-motor neurons, a selective subtype of SpMNs vulnerable in ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaplan et al., 2014 in the context of discussing differential motor neuron sensitivity.

claims.claim: Reduction of MMP-9 significantly delayed muscle denervation of fast-fatigable α-motor neurons in the ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1 G93A.
claims.source: Reduction of MMP-9 significantly delayed muscle denervation of fast-fatigable α-motor neurons in the ALS mouse model expressing hSOD1 G93A (Kaplan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kaplan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Expression of IGF-2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is upregulated in the resistant oculomotor neurons.
claims.source: Conversely, expression of IGF-2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) is upregulated in the resistant oculomotor neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allodi et al., 2016 in the context of discussing mechanisms of motor neuron resistance.

claims.claim: Viral delivery of IGF-2 to the muscles of hSOD1 G93A mice extended life-span by 10%.
claims.source: Viral delivery of IGF-2 to the muscles of hSOD1 G93A mice extended life-span by 10% (Allodi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Allodi et al., 2016.

claims.claim: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity.
claims.source: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity (Thaler et al., 2002), while Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation (Morin et al., 1997; Hirsch et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thaler et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation.
claims.source: During embryonic differentiation, Isl1 and Lhx3 transcription factors specify SpMN identity (Thaler et al., 2002), while Isl1 and Phox2a are essential for CrMN differentiation (Morin et al., 1997; Hirsch et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morin et al., 1997 and Hirsch et al., 2007.

claims.claim: A third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2%) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 in postnatal day 100 SOD1 G93A mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that a third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2% [mean ± SEM]; 195 motor neurons from three mice) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 while, by contrast, we were unable to detect any aggregation within O/TrMNs (328 motor neurons from three mice) (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data from P100 SOD1 G93A mice shown in Figure 1A-B.

claims.claim: No aggregation of misfolded hSOD1 was detected within O/TrMNs in postnatal day 100 SOD1 G93A mice.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that a third of all SpMNs (34 ± 4.2% [mean ± SEM]; 195 motor neurons from three mice) contain aggregates of misfolded hSOD1 while, by contrast, we were unable to detect any aggregation within O/TrMNs (328 motor neurons from three mice) (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunostaining data from P100 SOD1 G93A mice shown in Figure 1A-B.

claims.claim: O/TrMNs exhibited strikingly lower overall levels of misfolded hSOD1 compared to SpMNs, necessitating imaging under 5–10 times higher confocal laser intensity.
claims.source: Additionally, O/TrMNs exhibited strikingly lower overall levels of misfolded hSOD1 compared to SpMNs, necessitating imaging under 5–10 times higher confocal laser intensity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: By Day 5, 87% of iCrMNs and 74% of iSpMNs survived compared to Day 2.
claims.source: By Day 5, 87% of iCrMNs and 74% of iSpMNs survived compared to Day 2 (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: By Day 25, 52% of iCrMNs and 31% of iSpMNs survived.
claims.source: By Day 25, 52% of iCrMNs and 31% of iSpMNs survived.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: 88% of primary O/TrMNs and 72% of primary SpMNs survived on DIV 7.
claims.source: With the optimized supplement cocktail [10 ng/mL GDNF, 10 ng/mL BDNF, 10 ng/mL CNTF, 100 μM 3-isobutyl-1-methylxanthine (IBMX) and 10 μM Forskolin], 88% of primary O/TrMNs and 72% of primary SpMNs survived on DIV 7 (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: On DIV 14, 71% of primary O/TrMNs and only 42% of primary SpMNs survived.
claims.source: On DIV 14, 71% of primary O/TrMNs and only 42% of primary SpMNs survived.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: iSpMNs accumulated over two times more soluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A by Day 15 compared to Day 2.
claims.source: While iCrMNs maintained similar levels of soluble hSOD1 mutant proteins from Day two to Day 15, iSpMNs accumulated over two times more soluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A by Day 15 compared to Day 2 (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claims.claim: iSpMNs accumulated approximately 3 times more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A than iCrMNs on Day 15.
claims.source: Moreover, iSpMNs also accumulated ~3 times more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and G93A than iCrMNs on Day 15 (Figure 3B,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B,D.

claims.claim: 100 nM of MG-132 reduced proteasome activity by approximately 30% in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.
claims.source: 100 nM of MG-132 reduced proteasome activity by ~30% in both iCrMNs (68.27 ± 10.30% compared to DMSO) and iSpMNs (67.63 ± 9.49% compared to DMSO, iCrMNs versus iSpMNs p=0.47 by Student's t-test, n = 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements using Suc-LLVY-AMC hydrolysis assay.

claims.claim: iSpMNs accumulated approximately 2 fold more insoluble mutant hSOD1 when the proteasome was compromised by MG-132.
claims.source: iSpMNs accumulated ~2 fold more insoluble mutant hSOD1 when the proteasome was compromised (1.73 ± 0.21 fold more hSOD1 A4V, p=0.03; 1.93 ± 0.23 fold more hSOD1 G93A, p=0.02) (Figure 4C), suggesting that proteins that would have normally been degraded by the proteasome instead contributed to the insoluble aggregates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B-C comparing MG-132 and DMSO treated neurons.

claims.claim: iCrMNs accumulated approximately 8.5 fold more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and approximately 5.3 fold more insoluble hSOD1 G93A compared to DMSO control after MG-132 treatment.
claims.source: Revealingly, iCrMNs accumulated ~8.5 fold more insoluble hSOD1 A4V and ~5.3 fold more insoluble hSOD1 G93A compared to DMSO control (Figure 4B,C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claims.claim: MG-132 treatment resulted in accumulation of more soluble and insoluble p62 proteins in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs, with iSpMNs and iCrMNs accumulating 2–3 fold and 6–10 fold more insoluble p62 protein respectively.
claims.source: The mild reduction of proteasome activity resulted in accumulation of more soluble and insoluble p62 proteins in both iCrMNs and iSpMNs, with iSpMNs and iCrMNs accumulating 2–3 fold and 6–10 fold more insoluble p62 protein respectively (Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claims.claim: Over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions in hSOD1 G93A mice at postnatal days 66 and 97.
claims.source: While over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions, there were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-E from hSOD1 G93A mice.

claims.claim: There were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 in hSOD1 G93A mice at postnatal days 66 and 97.
claims.source: While over 40% of lumbar SpMNs accumulated p62 positive inclusions, there were no oculomotor neurons with protein aggregates containing p62 (Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-E from hSOD1 G93A mice.

claims.claim: More iSpMNs (approximately 15%) exhibited p62-positive cytoplasmic aggregates than did iCrMNs (approximately 5%) on Day 5.
claims.source: Consistent with in vivo observations, more iSpMNs (~15%) exhibited p62-positive cytoplasmic aggregates than did iCrMNs (~5%) (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Inhibition of the proteasome by MG-132 treatment resulted in nearly 50% of iCrMNs containing p62 aggregates, compared to approximately 30% of iSpMNs.
claims.source: Interestingly, inhibition of the proteasome by MG-132 treatment had a greater effect on iCrMNs, nearly 50% of which contained p62 aggregates, compared to ~30% of iSpMNs (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: 150 ng/ml tunicamycin was significantly more toxic to iSpMNs than to iCrMNs (65 ± 6% survival for iCrMNs and 47 ± 3% for iSpMNs).
claims.source: While 100 ng/ml tunicamycin affected both cell types nearly equally (88 ± 4% survival for iCrMNs and 83 ± 5% for iSpMNs, respectively), 150 ng/ml tunicamycin was significantly more toxic to iSpMNs than to iCrMNs (65 ± 6% survival for iCrMNs and 47 ± 3% for iSpMNs, respectively) (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: At 300 ng/mL tunicamycin, close to 50% (49% ± 5%) of iCrMNs survived compared to only about 10% (11% ± 1%) of iSpMNs.
claims.source: iCrMNs were consistently more resistant to tunicamycin up through the highest concentration tested (300 ng/mL), at which close to 50% (49% ± 5%) of iCrMNs survived compared to only about 10% (11% ± 1%) of iSpMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: 10 μM CPA treatment resulted in iCrMNs displaying an insensitivity to treatment (103 ± 6%) compared to only approximately 80% (75% ± 4%) of iSpMNs surviving.
claims.source: 10 μM CPA, however, was sufficient to reveal a survival difference, with iCrMNs displaying an insensitivity to treatment (103 ± 6%) compared to only ~80% (75% ± 4%) of iSpMNs surviving (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: At 40 μM CPA, the survival of iSpMNs was only about 10% (9% ± 1%) compared to nearly 40% (37% ± 3%) of iCrMNs.
claims.source: This differential survival trend was maintained through the highest concentration tested (40 μM), at which the survival of iSpMNs was only about 10% (9% ± 1%) compared to nearly 40% (37% ± 3%) of iCrMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: iSpMNs showed higher induction of sXBP1, GRP78 and ATF4 than iCrMNs after CPA treatment.
claims.source: iSpMNs showed higher induction of sXBP1, GRP78 and ATF4 than iCrMNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 measuring UPR markers after CPA treatment.

claims.claim: Brefeldin A was equally toxic to both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.
claims.source: Brefeldin A was equally toxic to both cell types (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml.
claims.source: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml and to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM (Figure 8B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM.
claims.source: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin treatment within 100–250 ng/ml and to CPA treatment within 10–25 µM (Figure 8B–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: iCrMNs contain higher levels of all 20S core subunits of the proteasome than iSpMNs.
claims.source: Among the differences, we noted that iCrMNs contain higher levels of all 20S core subunits of the proteasome than iSpMNs (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by unbiased mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Differences in proteasome subunit levels are not found among regulatory subunits of the proteasome.
claims.source: Interestingly, these differences are not found among regulatory subunits of the proteasome (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: Non-transgenic iCrMNs had a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs at Day 2 and 5 in culture.
claims.source: Non-transgenic iCrMNs had a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs at Day 2 and 5 in culture (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: PD169316 treatment increased chymotrypsin-like activity of the 20S proteasome in iSpMNs and iCrMNs in a dosage dependent manner.
claims.source: In agreement to what has been described in other neuronal cell types, PD169316 treatment increased chymotrypsin-like activity of the 20S proteasome in iSpMNs and iCrMNs in a dosage dependent manner (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by proteasome activity measurements shown in Figure 10B.

claims.claim: 0.25–2 μM PD169316 did not affect the survival of iCrMNs or iSpMNs in culture.
claims.source: 0.25–2 μM PD169316 did not affect the survival of iCrMNs or iSpMNs in culture (Figure 10C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10C.

claims.claim: Co-treatment of PD169316 improved the survival of iSpMNs from 66 ± 4% with no PD169316 to 80 ± 4% with 2 µM PD169316 in the presence of 10 µM CPA.
claims.source: In a concentration dependent manner, co-treatment of PD169316 improved the survival of iSpMNs from 66 ± 4% with no PD169316% to 80 ± 4% with 2 µM PD169316 (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: 0–2 μM PD169316 treatment did not significantly enhance iCrMN survival to 10 µM CPA.
claims.source: 0–2 μM PD169316 treatment did not significantly enhance iCrMN survival to 10 µM CPA (Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: Enhancing proteasome activity by 2 µM PD169316 was sufficient to increase iSpMN survival to phenocopy the basal iCrMN resistance to 10 µM CPA treatment.
claims.source: Notably, enhancing proteasome activity by 2 µM PD169316 was sufficient to increase iSpMN survival to phenocopy the basal iCrMN resistance to 10 µM CPA treatment (indicated by the red dash line in Figure 10D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10D.

claims.claim: PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls.
claims.source: These experiments revealed that PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls but showed no effects in iCrMNs (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10F using lentiviral expression of PSMB5.

claims.claim: PSMB5 expression showed no effects on iCrMN survival to CPA treatment.
claims.source: These experiments revealed that PSMB5 expression significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ infected controls but showed no effects in iCrMNs (Figure 10F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by survival assay data shown in Figure 10F.

claims.claim: CPA treatment significantly increased the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 A4V.
claims.source: CPA treatment significantly increased the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 A4V (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs regardless of DMSO or CPA treatment.
claims.source: iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs regardless of the treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The hSOD1 A4V and hSOD1 G93A transgenes were expressed at similar levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs on Day 7.
claims.source: The differential accumulation of hSOD1 proteins between iCrMNs and iSpMNs was not secondary to cell-specific silencing or upregulation of the transgene as both the hSOD1 A4V and hSOD1 G93A transgenes were expressed at similar levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs on Day 7, measured by RT-qPCR.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR measurements showing no significant difference in hSOD1 mRNA levels between iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claims.claim: The translation efficiency of hSOD1 was similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs as measured by polysome profiling.
claims.source: The translation efficiency of hSOD1 was also similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs as measured by polysome profiling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: iCrMNs have a cell-autonomous mechanism to restrain the accumulation of hSOD1 mutant proteins.
claims.source: Therefore, it is likely that iCrMNs have a cell-autonomous mechanism to restrain the accumulation of hSOD1 mutant proteins, and perhaps other misfolded proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hSOD1 mRNA and translation are similar between iCrMNs and iSpMNs, yet protein accumulation differs.

claims.claim: A substantial fraction of mutant hSOD1 protein is being targeted for degradation by the proteasome in iCrMNs.
claims.source: Thus, a substantial fraction of mutant hSOD1 protein is being targeted for degradation by the proteasome in iCrMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MG-132 treatment caused much greater accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in iCrMNs than iSpMNs.

claims.claim: iCrMNs may rely on the proteasome to a greater extent than iSpMNs to degrade mutant misfolded hSOD1 proteins and reduce their accumulation in insoluble aggregates.
claims.source: These results imply that iCrMNs may rely on the proteasome to a greater extent than iSpMNs to degrade mutant misfolded hSOD1 proteins and reduce their accumulation in insoluble aggregates.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential response to MG-132 treatment between iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claims.claim: There is an intrinsic difference between iCrMNs and iSpMNs in their use of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins that would otherwise contribute to insoluble protein aggregates.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that there is an intrinsic difference between iCrMNs and iSpMNs in their use of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins that would otherwise contribute to insoluble protein aggregates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the differential accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and p62 after MG-132 treatment shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: iSpMNs experienced a stronger level of proteostatic stress than iCrMNs to the same CPA treatment.
claims.source: This suggests that iSpMNs experienced a stronger level of proteostatic stress than iCrMNs to the same CPA treatment, presumably because they are less efficient than iCrMNs at degrading misfolded proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the higher induction of UPR markers in iSpMNs compared to iCrMNs after CPA treatment.

claims.claim: Additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins.
claims.source: These results suggest that additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins and that iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that CPA treatment increased insoluble hSOD1 A4V accumulation.

claims.claim: iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
claims.source: These results suggest that additional proteostatic stress accelerates the accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 mutant proteins and that iCrMNs maintain a superior capability to deal with misfolded proteins under CPA treatment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that iCrMNs accumulated less insoluble hSOD1 A4V than iSpMNs under both DMSO and CPA treatment.

claims.claim: Culture conditions do not favor iCrMNs' ability to resist all chemical stress.
claims.source: The comparable sensitivities of iCrMNs and iSpMNs to brefeldin A suggest that culture conditions do not favor iCrMNs' ability to resist all chemical stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that brefeldin A was equally toxic to both iCrMNs and iSpMNs.

claims.claim: ALS-resistant neuronal fate is associated with an intrinsically superior capacity to deal with generalized proteostatic stress.
claims.source: To test if ALS-resistant neuronal fate is associated with an intrinsically superior capacity to deal with generalized proteostatic stress, we compared the sensitivity of non-transgenic mouse primary ALS-resistant O/TrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs to tunicamycin and CPA.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that primary O/TrMNs were more resistant than primary SpMNs to proteostatic stress, confirming predictions from ESC-derived neurons.

claims.claim: The upregulation of core proteasome proteins in iCrMNs is due to post-transcriptional mechanisms.
claims.source: Of note, RNA-seq experiments did not reveal this difference, which seems to be due to post-transcriptional mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that proteomic data showed differences in proteasome subunit levels while RNA-seq did not.

claims.claim: iCrMNs have a higher capacity to degrade misfolding proteins and prevent the accumulation of insoluble aggregates because they have a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that iCrMN have a higher capacity to degrade misfolding proteins and prevent the accumulation of insoluble aggregates because they have a higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of proteomic data showing higher 20S core subunit levels and functional data showing higher proteasome activity in iCrMNs.

claims.claim: A superior proteostatic capacity could be an intrinsic and disease relevant mechanism underlying CrMN resistance to ALS.
claims.source: This superior proteostatic capacity could be an intrinsic and disease relevant mechanism underlying CrMN resistance to ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the convergence of in vitro ESC-derived neuron data, primary neuron data, and in vivo mouse model data.

claims.claim: ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 observed in vivo.
claims.source: By over-expressing hSOD1 mutant proteins, ESC-derived induced CrMNs (iCrMNs) and SpMNs (iSpMNs) recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in vitro and revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data comparing hSOD1 accumulation in iCrMNs and iSpMNs shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: ESC-derived neurons revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
claims.source: By over-expressing hSOD1 mutant proteins, ESC-derived induced CrMNs (iCrMNs) and SpMNs (iSpMNs) recapitulated the differential accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 in vitro and revealed more efficient proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins in iCrMNs than SpMNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by MG-132 treatment experiments shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: The ESC-based platform has predictive value for identifying cell-autonomous properties that contribute to cell specific differential vulnerability to ALS.
claims.source: Combining the results from hSOD1 G93A mice and primary motor neuron cultures, these data confirm our hypothesis generated from ESC-derived motor neurons that ALS-resistant CrMNs are more resistant to proteostatic stress than SpMNs. It also highlights the predictive value of this ESC-based in vitro platform for the study of cell-autonomous properties that contribute to the cell specific differential vulnerability to ALS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the concordance between ESC-derived neuron findings and in vivo/primary neuron validation.

claims.claim: CrMNs take better advantage of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins and maintain proteostasis.
claims.source: Therefore, our comparative study of ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs identified that CrMNs take better advantage of the ubiquitin proteasome system to degrade misfolded proteins and maintain proteostasis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including MG-132 experiments, proteasome activity measurements, and proteomic analysis.

claims.claim: Persistent activation of p38 was observed in motor neurons beginning in the presymptomatic stages of the disease in hSOD1 G93A mice.
claims.source: In hSOD1 G93A mice, persistent activation of p38 was observed in motor neurons beginning in the presymptomatic stages of the disease (Tortarolo et al., 2003; Holasek et al., 2005; Morfini et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tortarolo et al., 2003; Holasek et al., 2005; Morfini et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Chemical inhibition of p38 enhanced SpMN survival and rescued axonal transport defects.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background context for ALS pathology, including the differential vulnerability of motor neuron subtypes, the role of protein aggregation, and the involvement of protein degradation pathways. These claims are primarily based on prior literature and establish the scientific foundation for the study.
results.evaluation: These claims are well-supported by extensive citations to established literature (C1, C11-C27, C83-C91). They represent accepted knowledge in the ALS field and provide appropriate context for the experimental work. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with current understanding of ALS pathology.

results.result: In the hSOD1 G93A mouse model at postnatal day 100, approximately 34% of spinal motor neurons contain misfolded hSOD1 aggregates while oculomotor/trochlear motor neurons show no detectable aggregation and exhibit 5-10 times lower overall levels of misfolded hSOD1.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 and C8 are supported by quantitative immunostaining data from Figure 1A-B showing clear differences in hSOD1 aggregation between motor neuron subtypes. The sample size (n=3 mice, 195 SpMNs, 328 O/TrMNs) is adequate for this type of analysis. The imaging methodology accounts for differential signal intensity, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: In the hSOD1 G93A mouse model, over 40% of lumbar spinal motor neurons accumulated p62-positive inclusions while no oculomotor neurons contained p62 aggregates at postnatal days 66 and 97.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 and C9 are supported by immunostaining data in Figure 6D-E from hSOD1 G93A mice. The complete absence of p62 aggregates in oculomotor neurons (0%) versus >40% in SpMNs represents a striking difference. Sample size appears adequate (n=3 mice, ~100 cells per replicate).

results.result: ESC-derived iCrMNs show better survival than iSpMNs in culture (87% vs 74% at Day 5, 52% vs 31% at Day 25), recapitulating the differential survival observed in primary motor neurons (88% vs 72% O/TrMNs vs SpMNs at DIV 7, 71% vs 42% at DIV 14).
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 and C92 are supported by survival assay data in Figures 1D and 1G. The parallel survival differences between ESC-derived and primary neurons support the validity of the ESC model. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-8 biological replicates) and statistical significance is demonstrated.

results.result: Single-cell RNA sequencing analysis demonstrates that ESC-derived iCrMNs and iSpMNs resemble molecular features of ALS-resistant O/TrMNs and ALS-sensitive SpMNs respectively, supporting the validity of the ESC-based platform.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figures 1H-I and supplementary figures. The PCA analysis showing separation along PC2 (CrMN vs SpMN fate) and expression of appropriate fate markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) provide molecular validation of the cell identities. The analysis of 450 cells after quality control is adequate.

results.result: ESC-derived iSpMNs accumulated over 2-fold more soluble hSOD1 mutant proteins and approximately 3-fold more insoluble hSOD1 by Day 15 compared to iCrMNs, recapitulating differential accumulation observed in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36, C2, and C79 are supported by western blot data in Figure 3B-D. The quantification shows statistically significant differences (n=4 biological replicates). The use of both soluble and insoluble fractions strengthens the analysis. The differential accumulation despite similar transgene expression (C65) and translation efficiency (C66) supports a post-translational mechanism.

results.result: The differential accumulation of hSOD1 between iCrMNs and iSpMNs is not due to differences in transgene expression or translation efficiency, suggesting iCrMNs have a cell-autonomous mechanism to restrain hSOD1 accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by RT-qPCR data showing similar mRNA levels and polysome profiling data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) showing similar translation efficiency. However, the polysome profiling has only n=2 biological replicates, which is a limitation. The inference in C67 is reasonable given the data but represents a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: Treatment with 100 nM MG-132 (reducing proteasome activity by ~30%) caused iCrMNs to accumulate 5-8.5 fold more insoluble hSOD1 mutants compared to 2-fold in iSpMNs, revealing that iCrMNs rely more heavily on proteasomal degradation of misfolded hSOD1.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39, C68-C69, and C80 are supported by western blot data in Figure 4B-C. The differential response to MG-132 is striking and statistically significant (n=3). The use of a mild proteasome inhibition (30% reduction) is appropriate to avoid pleiotropic effects. The conclusion that iCrMNs rely more on proteasomal degradation is well-supported by the data.

results.result: MG-132 treatment resulted in greater accumulation of insoluble ubiquitinated proteins in iCrMNs (13-18 fold) compared to iSpMNs (3-5 fold), and iCrMNs accumulated 6-10 fold more insoluble p62 versus 2-3 fold in iSpMNs, demonstrating an intrinsic difference in proteasome system usage.
results.evaluation: Claims C40 and C70 are supported by western blot data in Figure 5B-E showing differential accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins and p62. The pattern mirrors the hSOD1 accumulation data, strengthening the conclusion that this is a general difference in proteostasis rather than specific to hSOD1. Sample size is adequate (n=3).

results.result: iSpMNs expressing mutant hSOD1 accumulated significantly more insoluble p62 than iCrMNs by Day 15, and approximately 15% of iSpMNs versus 5% of iCrMNs exhibited p62-positive aggregates on Day 5. MG-132 treatment increased p62 aggregates more in iCrMNs (to ~50%) than iSpMNs (~30%).
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C43-C44, and C96 are supported by western blot (Figure 6B-C) and immunocytochemistry data (Figure 6F). The differential accumulation of p62 is consistent with the hSOD1 and ubiquitin data. The greater effect of MG-132 on iCrMNs further supports their greater reliance on proteasomal degradation. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3, m~100 cells).

results.result: ESC-derived iCrMNs showed significantly greater resistance than iSpMNs to tunicamycin (49% vs 11% survival at 300 ng/mL) and CPA (37% vs 9% survival at 40 μM), demonstrating intrinsic resistance to chemically-induced proteostatic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 and C5 are supported by dose-response survival data in Figure 7B-C. The differential survival is consistent across multiple concentrations and statistically significant. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-6). The use of multiple ER stressors (tunicamycin, CPA, thapsigargin) strengthens the conclusion about general proteostatic stress resistance.

results.result: iSpMNs showed higher induction of UPR markers (sXBP1, GRP78, ATF4) than iCrMNs after CPA treatment, suggesting iSpMNs experienced stronger proteostatic stress due to less efficient protein degradation.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C71 are supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The differential UPR response provides molecular evidence for greater proteostatic stress in iSpMNs. Sample size is adequate (n=4). The inference in C71 is reasonable but represents an interpretation of the data.

results.result: Brefeldin A was equally toxic to both iCrMNs and iSpMNs, suggesting culture conditions do not favor iCrMNs' ability to resist all chemical stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C74 are supported by survival data in Figure 7E showing no significant difference between cell types. This negative control is important for demonstrating that the differential resistance is specific to proteostatic stress rather than a general artifact of culture conditions. Sample sizes are adequate (n=7-8).

results.result: CPA treatment significantly increased accumulation of insoluble hSOD1 A4V, but iCrMNs still accumulated less than iSpMNs regardless of treatment, demonstrating that iCrMNs maintain superior capability to handle misfolded proteins even under additional proteostatic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 and C72-C73 are supported by western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2. The maintenance of differential accumulation under stress conditions strengthens the conclusion about intrinsic differences in proteostatic capacity. Sample size is adequate (n=4).

results.result: Primary O/TrMNs were significantly more resistant than primary SpMNs to tunicamycin (100-250 ng/mL) and CPA (10-25 μM), confirming predictions from ESC-derived neurons and validating the ESC platform's predictive value.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52, C10, C75, and C81 are supported by survival data in Figure 8B-C from primary neurons. The concordance between ESC-derived and primary neuron responses is critical for validating the model system. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-4). This validation strengthens all conclusions drawn from the ESC system.

results.result: Mass spectrometry revealed that iCrMNs contain higher levels of all 20S proteasome core subunits but not 19S regulatory subunits compared to iSpMNs, with differences appearing to be due to post-transcriptional mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 9B, but the study has only n=2 biological replicates, which is insufficient for robust proteomic conclusions. Claim C76 about post-transcriptional mechanisms is inferred from the absence of RNA-seq differences, but no RNA-seq data are shown in the figures. Additional replicates and direct comparison of RNA and protein levels would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Non-transgenic iCrMNs had higher proteasome activity than iSpMNs at Day 2 and Day 5, suggesting iCrMNs have higher capacity to degrade misfolded proteins and prevent aggregate accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C4, and C77 are supported by proteasome activity measurements in Figure 9C using the Suc-LLVY-AMC assay. Sample size is adequate (n=6). The functional data complement the proteomic findings (C53-C54), though the proteomic data have limited replicates. The conclusion in C77 is a reasonable inference combining both datasets.

results.result: The p38 inhibitor PD169316 increased proteasome activity in a dose-dependent manner without affecting baseline survival (0.25-2 μM), and co-treatment with 2 μM PD169316 improved iSpMN survival to 10 μM CPA from 66% to 80%, phenocopying basal iCrMN resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 and C6 are supported by proteasome activity data (Figure 10B) and survival data (Figure 10C-D). The dose-response is well-characterized and sample sizes are adequate (n=4-6). The rescue of iSpMN sensitivity to match iCrMN resistance is a key finding supporting the proteasome hypothesis. However, PD169316 has multiple targets beyond p38, which is a limitation not fully addressed.

results.result: Lentiviral expression of PSMB5 significantly improved iSpMN survival to CPA treatment compared to LacZ controls but showed no effect in iCrMNs, providing genetic validation of the proteasome activation rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 and C7 are supported by survival data in Figure 10F using lentiviral PSMB5 expression. The genetic approach complements the pharmacological data (C56-C60) and addresses concerns about off-target effects. Sample size is adequate (n=4). The lack of effect in iCrMNs is consistent with their already high proteasome activity.

results.result: The authors conclude that superior proteostatic capacity through enhanced proteasome function is an intrinsic, disease-relevant mechanism underlying CrMN resistance to ALS, and that p38 inhibitor protective effects may benefit from enhanced proteasome activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C78, C82, and C85 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple lines of evidence: in vivo mouse data (C8-C9, C28-C30, C41-C42), ESC-derived neuron data (C35-C40, C45-C48, C53-C55), primary neuron validation (C51-C52), and rescue experiments (C56-C62). The convergence of evidence from multiple experimental systems strongly supports these conclusions, though C85 about p38 inhibitors is more speculative.

results.result: The authors infer that CrMN resistance to ALS neurodegeneration is not limited to SOD1-linked ALS based on non-transgenic iCrMNs being more resistant to general proteostatic stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 is supported by the observation that non-transgenic iCrMNs show greater resistance to tunicamycin and CPA (C45-C48) and higher proteasome activity (C55). This suggests the mechanism is intrinsic to cell fate rather than specific to SOD1 mutations. However, this remains an inference that would benefit from testing with other ALS-causing mutations.
